passA.summary: Patrick Collison, in a Startup School 2026 fireside with Harj Taggar, argues that AI is shifting startup strategy away from the classic lean-startup script of launching a narrow MVP and iterating into an adjacent niche. Because AI makes it cheap to spin up capability, he thinks founders should now start more ambitious, more 'decorrelated' companies up front — the pattern behind the labs, Anduril, and other recent winners — while noting Stripe itself took nearly two years to launch publicly but had a paying production user two months in. He pushes back on both the 'permanent underclass' panic driving students to drop out en masse and the fear that foundation-model labs will trample startups, citing Google's uneven record at prosecuting many priorities at once. The most concrete content is Stripe's own data: new businesses started on Stripe are up roughly 2x year-over-year, the median business is doing better than a year ago, and time-to-revenue for Atlas incorporations is falling. Worth watching for the data points and for a specific, contrarian read on where the lean-startup playbook still binds.
key_points: Collison frames knowledge as a cache hierarchy: even granting full model capability, retrieving a fact from your own 'cognitive L1 cache' is far faster than asking an agent, so students should not renounce learning things themselves before there's evidence the benefits are saturated.

He still writes everything himself and says he has never sent one of the AI-suggested replies that Gmail and WhatsApp now offer, because he finds model prose substantively deficient despite the models' ability to do monumental technical feats.

He dropped out of college twice, says the move is not a trapdoor since you can return, and argues the reputational cost is de minimis — but that his own sense of urgency about opportunities being fleeting was, in hindsight, a poor intuition.

Stripe seemed simultaneously obviously good (everyone hated existing payments) and obviously bad (two kids in fintech before 'fintech' was a word); grounding in a concrete, viscerally felt customer problem is what he credits with saving them.

Stripe waited ~2 years from first commit to public launch, which he thinks is wrong in most domains, but they had a live production user two months in and grew private beta every month, so they had continuous grounding in reality rather than hypotheses.

He argues the traditional lean-startup approach — buy Google Ads, find a crevice, expand from it — is now more aggressively tilled and competitive, and that AI makes it viable to start ambitious, divergent companies up front, citing the labs and Anduril as anti-lean-startup successes.

On fear of being crushed by the labs, he separates 'will model capabilities obviate this vertical' from 'will the labs build this'; on the latter he says the historical track record (Google) is checkered because organizations can't prosecute 100 priorities at once.

Stripe's data shows new business formation up roughly 2x year-over-year — the largest relative jump they've seen, exceeding the COVID-era ~50% inflection — with the median business performing better and time-to-revenue declining, which he reads as evidence against the 'vibe-coded slop' dismissal.

The main driver of faster startup growth is demand-side: incumbents now fear the risk of the status quo more than the risk of buying from an unproven startup, so enterprise contracts land far earlier in a company's life.
Against the thesis that AI is a hegemonic, centralizing force, he says Stripe's trend lines point toward a more decentralized world with many thousands of winners and more broad-based prosperity.

positions.claim: Even granting full model capability, human recall is materially faster than querying an agent, so students should keep learning things themselves rather than outsourcing cognition.
Companies at the frontier — Stripe and the labs alike — still pay an enormous premium for raw cognitive ability, which is revealed-preference evidence against renouncing learning.
LLMs have not yet produced a genuinely compelling essay, likely because the reward signal for good writing is hard to define for RL.
Dropping out of college carries essentially zero long-term reputational cost, and is reversible — he did it twice and returned in between.
His youthful belief that startup opportunities were fleeting was wrong; Silicon Valley has reliably had a surfeit of opportunities over many decades.
The current moment is not the last window to start a company — he'd take the under on that claim, comparing the panic to millenarian reactions like post-aviation utopianism.
Grounding in a concrete, viscerally felt customer problem is what makes a hard, unglamorous idea survivable; imagined customer problems are the failure mode.

A long pre-launch period is acceptable only if you have a continuous stream of real production users; Stripe waited two years to launch but had a paying customer two months in and added customers every month.
In most domains other than heavily regulated infrastructure, waiting two years to launch is the wrong call.
The classic lean-startup path of finding a small niche via ads and expanding is becoming more competitive and crowded, so founders should aggressively decorrelate instead.
Many of the most successful companies of the last decade — the labs, Anduril — are explicitly anti-lean-startup in how they began.
Lean startup dominated 20 years ago because of capital constraints and the absence of AI; AI now makes standing up a broad-capability organization cheap enough to start ambitious up front.
Founders should evaluate the success case, not just the failure case, before raising significant money — whether they want to do this work for 10, 17, or 30 years.
Fear that the big labs will expand into and crush startup ideas is overstated, because large organizations cannot successfully prosecute 100 priorities at once — as Google's checkered record shows.
Improving model capabilities will genuinely obviate some specific verticals and tasks, and already has in certain domains — a distinct risk from the labs competing directly.
New businesses started on Stripe are up around 2x year-over-year, the largest relative jump Stripe has recorded, versus roughly 50% during the 2020 COVID inflection.

The surge in new businesses is not just low-quality vibe-coded output: the median business is performing better than a year ago, probability of hitting revenue thresholds is rising, and Atlas time-to-revenue is declining.
Startup growth is accelerating primarily because incumbents now perceive the risk of the status quo as higher than the risk of adopting unproven vendors.
AI will not centralize the economy into a small number of winners; the trend lines point to many thousands of winners and more broad-based prosperity.
A business with many operational schleps can still be intellectually rich, because each customer is an applied theory about how some part of the world works.
